subject: Chemistry
title: The Demon Core: A Deadly Experiment
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Demon Core: A Deadly Experiment.

hook.text: A 6.2 kg sphere of plutonium killed two scientists in separate accidents. It was called the Demon Core.

buildup.text: Scientists at Los Alamos tested how close the plutonium could get to going critical by stacking neutron reflectors around it.

discovery.text: In 1945, Harry Daghlian dropped a brick of tungsten onto the core. It went briefly supercritical. He died 25 days later.

twist.text: In 1946, Louis Slotin used a screwdriver to hold apart two half-spheres around the core. It slipped. He died in 9 days.

climax.text: Slotin's body absorbed 1,000 rads of radiation instantly. He shielded others in the room, likely saving their lives.

punchline.text: A screwdriver between life and death. Two fatal accidents, one sphere of plutonium.

quiz.question: What caused the second Demon Core accident?
options: A screwdriver holding apart neutron reflectors slipped, causing a criticality burst
The plutonium sphere was dropped during transport
A miscalculated experiment triggered a chain reaction

details.summary: The Demon Core was a 6.2-kilogram plutonium sphere at Los Alamos that killed two scientists in separate criticality accidents in 1945 and 1946. Both incidents occurred during hands-on experiments that briefly pushed the core to supercriticality, releasing lethal bursts of neutron radiation.
details.whyItMatters: The Demon Core accidents established the dangers of criticality in nuclear materials handling and led to strict remote-operation protocols that govern nuclear work today.
takeaways: Two scientists died from separate criticality accidents with the same core
Louis Slotin held a screwdriver separating beryllium hemispheres by hand
The accidents ended hands-on criticality experiments permanently

faq.question: What is a criticality accident in nuclear physics?
faq.answer: A criticality accident occurs when fissile material like plutonium or enriched uranium unexpectedly reaches a self-sustaining chain reaction. This produces an intense burst of radiation in microseconds. The dose can be lethal even though the assembly does not explode like a bomb.

faq.question: Why were scientists handling a plutonium core with a screwdriver?
faq.answer: Early nuclear research had a cavalier safety culture. The experiment, called tickling the dragon's tail, involved manually lowering a beryllium reflector around the plutonium core. Slotin used a screwdriver as a spacer. When it slipped, the core went critical for a fraction of a second.
